resumo_pt: A avó tinha uma regra: em noite de chuva, ninguém conta em voz alta, e sempre se põe um prato a mais na ponta da mesa. Depois que ela morre, os netos passam um fim de semana na casa. Numa noite de tempestade, o cunhado cético conta em voz alta 'um, dois, três' e uma voz igual à dele responde 'quatro'. A luz apaga e eles ouvem alguém comendo a noite toda. Um caderno da avó revela: se alguém conta em voz alta, a coisa aprende a voz e vai embora com quem falou. Meses depois, numa foto do casal com quatro pratos, o reflexo da janela mostra alguém sentado na cadeira vazia.
descricao:
My grandmother had one rule about rain: never count out loud.

Would you have counted?

A new horror story from Veil Frequency. Fictional story. Images are AI-generated.

#horror #scarystories #horrorstory
tags: scary stories to fall asleep to

partes.visual: an old lonely farmhouse at night in heavy rain, one warm kitchen window lit, dark fields around

falas.text: My grandmother had exactly one rule about rain, and she never explained it.

When it rained at night, nobody in her house counted out loud. Not the dishes, not the stairs, not the people at the table. You could count anything you liked in your head, she said, but the moment a number left your mouth, you were asking a question. And she did not want to hear what answered.

partes.visual: an old wooden kitchen table set for dinner, at the far end a single extra place setting: one plate, one fork, one glass of water, empty chair, candlelight, rain on the window

falas.text: There was one more thing. On every stormy night, she set an extra place at the end of the table. One plate, one fork, one glass of water. She never looked at it. She never spoke of it. In the morning, the plate was clean and dry, and she washed it herself, as if it had been used.
When we were kids, my sister Nora and I thought it was an old woman's habit. We grew up, we moved away, and the rule became a family joke. Careful, don't count out loud. We laughed.

partes.visual: a farmhouse at the end of a muddy dirt road under dark storm clouds in late afternoon, empty fields, a car parked in front

falas.text: My grandmother died in October, at eighty-nine, in her sleep. The house came to the two of us. Nora, her husband Dan, and I spent a weekend there to empty it out before we sold.

The house sat at the end of a dirt road, twenty minutes from the nearest town. By Saturday afternoon, the sky had gone dark. By the time we sat down to eat in the kitchen, with food Dan had brought from town, the rain was coming down hard on the roof.

partes.visual: three adults eating dinner at an old farmhouse kitchen table at night, dim yellow light, rain streaking the dark window, an empty chair at the far end in shadow

falas.text: I counted without meaning to. Only in my head, the way she taught me. Nora. Dan. Me.
Three.
And then, at the corner of my eye, at the end of the table where my grandmother's chair always stood, I counted one more.
Four.

partes.visual: close-up of an old empty wooden chair at the end of a kitchen table in deep shadow, the air around it feels occupied, faint candlelight

falas.text: I did not look. It was the first thing my body remembered: never look. I sat there with my fork frozen in my hand, listening to the rain. There was no sound from that end of the table. But the chair at the end, which had been empty when we sat down, suddenly felt occupied, the way a room feels when someone has just left it.

I stood up slowly. I opened the cabinet where she kept the good dishes. I took out a plate, a fork, a glass. I poured water from the pitcher. I set everything at the end of the table, without looking at the chair, and sat back down.
Nobody spoke. Nora had stopped eating. She was watching me, and I saw her face change. She remembered. Without a word, she stood, took a folded napkin, and laid it beside the plate.

partes.visual: a skeptical man in his thirties leaning back at a dinner table with crossed arms and a small mocking smile, two worried women beside him, dim kitchen light

falas.text: Dan laughed.
Okay. What is this? Is this a family thing?
Eat, Nora said quietly.
You two are grieving, I get it. But you're setting a plate for nobody.

It's not for nobody, I said. It's Grandma's rule. When it rains, if there's one more than there should be, you set the plate. You don't look, you don't speak, you don't count. It leaves when the rain stops.
Dan looked at me, then at Nora. He waited for one of us to smile. Neither of us did.
You're serious.
Dan, Nora said. Please. Don't count.

It was the please that got to him. I watched it happen. He was a rational man, and a rational man cannot stand to be told to obey a rule with no reason. He leaned back in his chair, crossed his arms, and said with a small, unkind smile:

partes.visual: a man at a dark dinner table pointing his finger as he counts, faces of two frightened women, the far end of the table lost in black shadow

falas.text: One. Two. Three.
He pointed at each of us. At Nora. At me. At himself.
See? Three. There's nobody at the end of the
Four.

The voice came from the end of the table. Low and dry, like a sheet of paper being turned. And I recognized the sound of it, and my stomach dropped: it was Dan's voice. Exactly Dan's voice, only half a second late, like an echo that had learned to speak on its own.
The lights went out.

partes.visual: almost total darkness in a farmhouse kitchen, only rain on the window faintly lit, two trembling hands holding each other under a table

falas.text: Nobody moved. The rain pounded the roof, and the darkness in the kitchen was total. I felt Nora's hand find mine under the table. It was ice cold, and shaking.
Don't look, she whispered. Don't look, don't look.
I heard Dan breathing fast. I heard him murmur, I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.
And then I heard the fork.

partes.visual: close-up of an old silver fork resting on a white porcelain plate in near darkness, faint gleam of light, unsettling stillness

falas.text: A soft clink of metal on porcelain. Then another. Someone at the end of the table was eating.

We sat there all night. I can't tell you how long it lasted. I counted my sister's breaths in my head, only in my head, until I lost the count. At some point, the sound of the fork stopped. But the rain kept going, and we kept not looking.

partes.visual: gray morning light through a kitchen window after rain, a clean dry white plate with a fork lined up beside it and an empty glass, the chair pushed in neatly

falas.text: When the gray light of morning came through the kitchen window, the rain had stopped.
I looked first. The plate was clean and dry. The fork lay lined up beside it. The glass was empty. The chair was pushed in against the table, as if no one had ever stood up from it.

partes.visual: an old worn notebook held with a rubber band in a dusty pantry behind jars of preserves, open pages full of handwritten dates and tally marks in blue ink

falas.text: That was the morning we found the notebook. It was in the pantry, behind the jars of preserves, held shut with an old rubber band. My grandmother's handwriting, in blue ink, page after page. One line for every storm. Fifty years of lines. A date, and next to each date, a tally mark.
On the last page, the handwriting was shakier, written not long before she died.
The plate holds it for one night. But if anyone counts out loud, it learns the voice. It doesn't leave with the rain. It leaves with whoever spoke.
Nora read it aloud, and then covered her mouth, realizing what she had done. But it wasn't raining, and nothing answered.

partes.visual: a pale exhausted man staring through a car window at night, rain drops on the glass, haunted eyes

falas.text: Dan didn't speak during breakfast. He didn't speak on the drive home. When we dropped him off, he looked at me through the car window and said:
I can still hear it.
That was six months ago. Nora calls me sometimes. She says Dan sets four plates at the table every night, rain or not. She says it's easier to feed it than to hear it ask.

partes.visual: a family photo of three smiling adults at a dinner table with four plates and four chairs, a dark window behind them reflecting a fourth shadowy figure sitting at the empty chair

falas.text: Last week she sent me a photo of their table. Four plates, four chairs, and the three of them smiling at the camera. I stared at it and counted, in my head, the way my grandmother taught me.
Three.
Then I noticed the window behind them. In the reflection in the glass, at the end of the table, where the photo showed an empty chair, someone else was sitting. I counted the reflection.
Four.
I haven't counted anything out loud since.
